units.title: Amazing animal homes

words.def: a hole or tunnel in the ground that an animal digs to live in
words.ex: The rabbit ran into its ___ when it saw the fox.

words.def: a place that keeps you safe from bad weather or danger
words.ex: The cave gave the bats ___ from the wind and rain.

words.def: a large group of the same kind of animal that live together
words.ex: A ___ of ants can have millions of members.

words.def: a home where bees live and make honey
words.ex: The bees flew back to their ___ with pollen on their legs.

words.def: a wall built across a river to hold back the water
words.ex: Beavers build a ___ of sticks and mud across the stream.

words.def: an animal that hunts and eats other animals
words.ex: The owl is a ___ that hunts mice at night.

words.def: to keep someone or something safe from harm
words.ex: Thick walls of mud ___ the chicks from the hot sun.

words.def: to stay alive, especially in a difficult situation
words.ex: Camels can ___ for many days without drinking water.

words.def: empty inside
words.ex: The woodpecker made its home in a ___ tree.

words.def: below the surface of the earth
words.ex: Moles spend most of their lives ___, digging tunnels in the dark.

words.def: to build something, such as a house, a bridge or a nest
words.ex: Weaver birds ___ their nests by tying knots in grass.

words.def: the natural place where an animal or plant usually lives
words.ex: The rainforest is the natural ___ of many colourful frogs.

words.def: to spend the winter in a kind of deep sleep, as some animals do
words.ex: Hedgehogs ___ in piles of dry leaves until the spring.

words.def: active at night and asleep during the day
words.ex: Most owls are ___ birds, so they hunt when it is dark.

words.def: to travel to a different part of the world at the same time every year
words.ex: Every autumn, swallows ___ to Africa to find warmer weather and more insects.

words.def: an area that an animal treats as its own and defends from others
words.ex: A robin sings loudly to warn other robins to stay out of its ___.

words.def: a small room or space, for example one deep inside a nest or a burrow
words.ex: The queen ant lays her eggs in a special ___ deep under the ground.

words.def: the door, gate or opening that you use to go into a place
words.ex: The ___ to the rabbit's burrow was hidden under a bush.

words.def: to need someone or something and trust them to help you
words.ex: Baby birds ___ on their parents for food and warmth.

words.def: very difficult to live in, for example extremely cold, dry or windy
words.ex: Emperor penguins survive the ___ winters of Antarctica.

grammar.q: Scientists ___ a new kind of spider web last year.
grammar.why: 'Last year' is a finished time, so use the past simple: found.

grammar.q: Owls ___ in that old barn since last winter.
grammar.why: With 'since', use the present perfect for something that started in the past and is still true now.

grammar.q: Most bird nests ___ from twigs, grass and mud.
grammar.why: The nests don't make anything; birds make them. Use the passive: are + made (plural, because 'nests').

grammar.q: This old wasp nest ___ in our garden last summer.
grammar.why: Someone found the nest at a finished time, so use the past passive. 'Nest' is singular, so use 'was'.

grammar.q: A beaver is an animal ___ builds dams across rivers.
grammar.why: Use 'which' (or 'that') to give more information about an animal or a thing.

grammar.q: This is the cave ___ thousands of bats sleep in winter.
grammar.why: Use 'where' after a place when a full sentence follows (bats sleep there).

grammar.q: There ___ be a pond in this field, and lots of frogs lived in it.
grammar.why: 'Used to' + verb talks about something that was true in the past but is not true now.

grammar.q: A hermit crab is an animal ___ home is an old shell from a sea snail.
grammar.why: Use 'whose' to show that something belongs to someone or something: the crab's home.

grammar.q: Moles are very good at ___ tunnels.
grammar.why: After a preposition such as 'at', use the -ing form of the verb: good at digging.

grammar.q: If you ___ too close to the nest, the birds will fly away.
grammar.why: First conditional: if + present simple (go), then will + verb. Don't use 'will' after 'if' here.

sentences: Beavers have built dams across the river.
Termite mounds are built by millions of insects.
Has the bee colony survived the winter?
This is the tree where the owls live.
Hedgehogs hibernate in piles of dry leaves.
Swallows used to build their nests in our barn.

reading.title: Animal builders
reading.text:
Humans are not the only great builders. Many animals make amazing homes, and some of them work together in huge teams.

Beavers are famous for their dams. They cut down small trees with their strong teeth and push sticks, stones and mud together across a stream. The water behind the dam becomes a quiet pond. In the middle of it, the beavers build a home called a lodge. Its door is under the water, so most predators cannot get in.

The male weaver bird uses his beak to tie knots in long pieces of grass. If a female does not like the nest he has made, he may pull it apart and start again.

Termites are tiny insects, but their mounds can be taller than an adult. Inside, there are lots of tunnels. They let air move through the mound and help to keep the colony cool.

qs.q: Why is the door of a beaver lodge under the water?
opts: to stop the pond from freezing

qs.q: Beavers use only sticks to build their dams.
Weaver birds build a new nest every year.
Some termite homes are higher than a grown-up person.
What do the tunnels inside a termite mound do?
opts: They help to keep the mound cool.
They store food for the winter.
They join it to other mounds.

reading.title: The bird apartment block
reading.text:
In the dry Kalahari Desert of southern Africa, you may see something strange in a tree: a huge pile of grass that looks like a haystack. In fact, it is the home of a whole colony of small brown birds called sociable weavers.

Unlike most birds, sociable weavers build one giant nest together. The biggest nests can be several metres wide and hold more than a hundred birds. Inside, each pair has its own small chamber, and the entrance to it is a short tunnel underneath.

The nest is also a clever shelter from the harsh weather. Desert days are very hot, but winter nights can be freezing. The thick walls of grass keep the chambers cool during the day and warm at night.

Some of these nests are used for more than a hundred years. The birds keep repairing them and adding fresh grass, so they slowly grow bigger and bigger.

qs.q: Why might someone think the nest is a haystack?
opts: It is a huge pile of grass.
It is full of farm animals.
It is very small and yellow.

qs.q: Sociable weavers usually build their nests alone.
Each pair of birds has a room of its own inside the nest.
Other kinds of birds sometimes live in these nests too.
How do the thick walls of grass help the birds?
opts: They keep the chambers cool by day and warm at night.
They hide the birds from people.
They give the birds food in winter.

extra.q: Birds ___ a nest in spring.
extra.why: We say 'build a nest' (or 'make a nest'). We never 'do' or 'take' a nest.

extra.q: Many animals depend ___ their homes to stay safe.
extra.why: 'Depend on' is a fixed pair: the verb 'depend' is followed by 'on'.

extra.q: Thick fur gives the animal ___ from the cold. (protect)
extra.why: After 'gives the animal' we need a noun (a thing it gets): protection.

extra.q: Both parents ___ the eggs until the chicks hatch.
extra.why: 'Look after' means take care of someone or something.

extra.q: Hedgehogs hibernate in winter ___ there are very few insects for them to eat.
extra.why: 'Because' gives the reason: why do hedgehogs hibernate? There is not enough food for them.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'Many swallows return to the same nest every spring'?
opts: Every spring, many swallows come back to their old nest.
Many swallows build a new nest every spring.
Many swallows leave their nest in spring.
Swallows only use a nest once.
extra.why: 'Return to' means 'come back to', and 'the same nest' is their old nest.

sents: Many animals are skilful builders that make clever homes.
For example, beavers build dams across streams with sticks, stones and mud.
The dam turns the stream into a quiet pond, where they build a lodge.
Its entrance is under the water, so most predators cannot get in.
In this way, a beaver's home keeps the whole family safe.
Winter is a difficult time for many animals because food is hard to find.
Some animals, such as swallows, solve this problem by migrating to warmer countries.
Others, such as hedgehogs, stay where they are and hibernate until the spring.
While they sleep, their hearts beat much more slowly, so they use very little energy.
Both ways help these animals to survive until the weather gets warmer.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'Bees live together in hives, and thousands of them share the work. Termites build huge mounds with tunnels that keep the whole colony cool.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Some insects live and work together in very large groups.
I think insects are really cool!
Many birds build their nests in trees.
writing.why: The paragraph gives two examples of insects living in big groups, so the topic sentence must cover both. The others are too narrow, too chatty or about birds.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'The mole made a big hole under the ground.'?
opts: The mole dug a long tunnel underground.
The mole did a big hole under the ground.
The mole made a really, really big hole.
The mole made a thing under the ground.
writing.why: 'Dug' and 'tunnel' are exact words. 'Did a hole' is wrong, 'really, really' is chatty and 'a thing' is vague.

units.title: Great inventions

words.def: to make or design something that has never existed before
words.ex: Do you think someone will ever ___ a car that can fly?

words.def: a person who plans and builds machines, roads or bridges
words.ex: The ___ checked every part of the bridge before it opened.

words.def: a small machine or tool made for a special job
words.ex: A smartwatch is a tiny ___ that you wear on your wrist.

words.def: a kind of energy that gives power to lights and machines
words.ex: Before ___, people used candles and oil lamps to light their homes.

words.def: the part of a car, train or plane that makes it move
words.ex: The car's ___ was so quiet that I couldn't hear it.

words.def: a small object that stores power for things like torches and phones
words.ex: My torch stopped working because the ___ was flat.

words.def: a tool that makes very small things look much bigger
words.ex: Under the ___, a drop of pond water was full of tiny living things.

words.def: to plan and draw how something will look and work
words.ex: Engineers ___ new cars on computers before they build them.

words.def: to make something better
words.ex: Scientists keep trying to ___ batteries so that they last longer.

words.def: to take the place of something, or to put something new in its place
words.ex: Will robots ___ waiters in restaurants one day?

words.def: a test that scientists do to find out or prove something
words.ex: Every failed ___ taught the inventor something new.

words.def: useful and sensible for real life
words.ex: Rubber boots are a ___ choice for a muddy walk.

words.def: what something is made from, such as wood, metal, glass or plastic
words.ex: Plastic is a cheap ___ that can be made into almost any shape.

words.def: the hot gas that water turns into when it boils
words.ex: In the 1800s, many trains and ships were powered by ___.

words.def: a long, thin piece of metal that electricity can travel along
words.ex: The bulb is joined to the battery by a thin copper ___.

words.def: to make a machine work, or to control it
words.ex: Only trained workers are allowed to ___ this huge machine.

words.def: useful and easy for you, because it saves time or fits your plans
words.ex: The new bus stop is very ___ for us because it is right outside our house.

words.def: a person who is extremely clever or skilful
words.ex: Leonardo da Vinci was a ___ who drew plans for flying machines.

words.def: a try at doing something, especially something difficult
words.ex: His first ___ to build a robot ended in a pile of broken parts.

words.def: correct and exact, with no mistakes
words.ex: Atomic clocks are so ___ that they lose less than a second in millions of years.

grammar.q: The telephone ___ by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876.
grammar.why: The telephone didn't invent anything; Bell invented it. Use the past passive: was + invented.

grammar.q: People ___ wash their clothes by hand before washing machines were invented.
grammar.why: 'Used to' + verb talks about a past habit that is not true now.

grammar.q: My sister enjoys ___ robots out of old boxes.
grammar.why: After 'enjoy', use the -ing form of the verb.

grammar.q: The inventor decided ___ a smaller, cheaper machine.
grammar.why: After 'decide', use 'to' + verb.

grammar.q: Smartphones ___ the way we live since they first appeared.
grammar.why: With 'since', use the present perfect: the change started in the past and is still true now.

grammar.q: Have you ever ___ a 3D printer?
grammar.why: The present perfect is have + past participle: have you ever used...?

grammar.q: 'This machine doesn't work,' said the engineer. The engineer said that the machine ___ work.
grammar.why: In reported speech, the present (doesn't) usually moves one step back to the past (didn't).

grammar.q: Thomas Edison kept ___ until his light bulb worked.
grammar.why: After 'keep' (meaning continue), use the -ing form: kept trying.

grammar.q: In the 1940s, the first computers ___ as big as a room.
grammar.why: 'In the 1940s' is a finished time in the past, so use the past simple: were.

grammar.q: If I ___ a time machine, I would travel back to see the dinosaurs.
grammar.why: This is imaginary (second conditional), so use the past simple after 'if' (had), then would + verb.

sentences: Velcro was invented by a Swiss engineer.
My grandparents used to write letters to each other.
He decided to build a machine that cleans windows.
Have you ever used a microscope at school?
The first trains were pulled by steam engines.
The engineer said that the machine didn't work.

reading.title: Happy accidents
reading.text:
Some of the world's most useful inventions were not planned at all.

In 1941, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral went for a walk in the mountains with his dog. When they got home, both of them were covered in tiny seeds from a plant. He looked at the seeds under a microscope and saw hundreds of little hooks. These hooks caught on the loops in cloth and fur. De Mestral decided to copy the idea. After years of experiments, he invented Velcro, which is now used on shoes, bags and even space suits.

A few years later, an American engineer called Percy Spencer was working with a machine that made radio waves. He noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Next, he tried some popcorn, and it popped! This led to the first microwave oven. It was nearly as tall as a person, so it was not very practical for a kitchen.

Both inventors noticed something small and asked, 'Why did that happen?'

qs.q: What did de Mestral see under the microscope?
De Mestral invented Velcro soon after his walk.
Velcro is more popular today than buttons.
The first microwave oven was too big to be useful in most homes.
What is the main idea of the text?
opts: Some great inventions began with a lucky surprise.
Engineers should always work in the mountains.
Velcro is better than the microwave oven.
Most inventions take only a few days to make.

reading.title: How the bicycle grew up
reading.text:
The first bicycle did not have any pedals. In 1817, a German inventor called Karl Drais built a wooden 'running machine'. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along the road with their feet.

In the 1860s, pedals were added to the front wheel. Makers soon realised that a bigger front wheel carried the bike further with each turn of the pedals. This led to the penny-farthing, which had a huge front wheel and a tiny back one. It was fast, but the seat was so high that riders often fell off.

The 'safety bicycle' of the 1880s solved this problem. Its two wheels were almost the same size, and a chain joined the pedals to the back wheel, just like on a bike today. A few years later, air-filled rubber tyres made riding much more comfortable.

Since then, bikes have been improved again and again, but the basic design has hardly changed in more than a hundred years.

qs.q: The first bicycle had pedals on its front wheel.
Karl Drais's running machine was made of wood.
The penny-farthing cost more than the safety bicycle.
Why did the penny-farthing have such a big front wheel?
opts: It made the bike go further with each turn of the pedals.
It helped riders to see over walls.
It made the seat more comfortable.
It made the bike easier to get on.

qs.q: What does the writer say about bikes today?
opts: Their basic design is very like the safety bicycle's.
They have a huge front wheel.
Riders push them along with their feet.
They are still made of wood.

extra.q: Inventors often ___ mistakes before they get things right.
extra.why: We say 'make a mistake', not 'do a mistake'.

extra.q: The first microwave oven was very big, ___ it was not practical for homes.
extra.why: 'So' shows a result: the oven was big, and the result was that it didn't suit homes.

extra.q: The telephone was an amazing ___. (invent)
extra.why: We need a noun for a thing: invention. An 'inventor' is a person.

extra.q: When the machine broke, the engineer tried to ___ what was wrong.
extra.why: 'Find out' means discover a fact or learn something new.

extra.q: Rubber is used ___ making tyres and boots.
extra.why: 'Used for' + -ing tells us what job something does: rubber is used for making tyres.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The microwave oven was invented by accident'?
opts: Nobody planned to invent the microwave oven.
The microwave oven caused an accident.
The microwave oven was invented on purpose.
The microwave oven was invented by a doctor.
extra.why: 'By accident' means without planning it, so nobody planned the invention.

sents: The printing press was one of the most important inventions in history.
Before it was invented, every book had to be copied by hand.
This was so slow that books were rare and very expensive.
In the 1440s, Johannes Gutenberg built a machine that could print pages quickly.
As a result, books became cheaper, and many more people learnt to read.
Mobile phones have changed a great deal since the first models appeared.
The earliest ones were heavy and could only be used to make calls.
Later, engineers added screens, cameras and access to the internet.
As a result, a modern smartphone can do the job of many devices, such as a camera, a map and a torch.
It is hard to imagine what phones will be able to do next.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people think that modern inventions make our lives easier. Do you agree or disagree?' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I agree that modern inventions make our lives easier, because they save time and help us to stay in touch.
Inventions are things that people make.
Some inventions are good and some are bad, so it depends.
My grandmother has a washing machine.
writing.why: A thesis gives a clear answer to the question and a reason. The others do not answer it, are too vague or tell a story.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'The new machine is very good because it does things fast.'?
opts: The new machine is useful because it completes tasks quickly.
The new machine is super good and really fast.
The new machine is nice because it does stuff fast.
The new machine is good because it does things.
writing.why: 'Useful' and 'completes tasks quickly' are precise. 'Super', 'stuff' and 'does things' are vague or chatty.

units.title: Healthy habits

words.def: the kind of food that you usually eat
words.ex: A healthy ___ includes plenty of fruit and vegetables.

words.def: with the right amount of each different thing
words.ex: A ___ lunch has a bit of everything: bread, cheese, salad and fruit.

words.def: something in food that your body needs in small amounts to stay healthy
words.ex: Oranges and kiwis are full of ___ C.

words.def: healthy and strong, especially because of exercise
words.ex: My aunt cycles to work every day to stay ___.

words.def: a part of the body that tightens and loosens to make you move
words.ex: Your heart is a ___ that works all day and all night.

words.def: something you do often, almost without thinking
words.ex: Brushing your teeth twice a day is a good ___.

words.def: to stay away from something, or to try not to do it
words.ex: Try to ___ sugary drinks between meals.

words.def: to take air into your body and let it out again
words.ex: During a race, runners ___ faster and more deeply.

words.def: to rest and become calm
words.ex: Reading a good book helps me ___ before bed.

words.def: worried and tense because of problems or too much work
words.ex: I felt ___ before the test, so I took some slow, deep breaths.

words.def: to not do something that you usually do
words.ex: It's not a good idea to ___ breakfast before a busy day at school.

words.def: the usual things you do each day, in the same order
words.ex: My bedtime ___ is a bath, a story and then lights out.

words.def: the way a person lives, for example what they eat and how active they are
words.ex: Walking to school every day is part of a healthy ___.

words.def: a good or helpful result that you get from something
words.ex: One ___ of cycling to school is that you get fresh air and exercise.

words.def: causing damage or making someone ill
words.ex: Strong sunshine can be ___ to your skin, so wear sun cream.

words.def: the amount of a food that is served to one person at one time
words.ex: A small ___ of chips is plenty for one person.

words.def: having enough water in your body
words.ex: On hot days, carry a water bottle so that you stay ___.

words.def: to give all your attention to one thing
words.ex: It's hard to ___ on your homework when the TV is on.

words.def: the way you feel at a particular time, for example happy or cross
words.ex: A walk in the sunshine always puts me in a good ___.

words.def: to become healthy again after you have been ill or hurt
words.ex: After a long run, your muscles need time to ___.

grammar.q: If you ___ enough sleep, you will feel tired at school.
grammar.why: In the first conditional, use the present simple after 'if' (don't get), and 'will' in the other half.

grammar.q: If you drink more water, you ___ better.
grammar.why: This is a real possibility in the future: if + present simple, then will + verb.

grammar.q: If I ___ a famous chef, I would cook healthy food for every school.
grammar.why: This is imaginary (second conditional), so use a past form after 'if'. 'If I were' is correct.

grammar.q: If we walked to school, we ___ fitter.
grammar.why: Second conditional: if + past simple, then would + verb (would be).

grammar.q: When I was little, I ___ hate vegetables, but now I love them.
grammar.why: 'Used to' + verb is for something that was true in the past but is not true now.

grammar.q: Try to avoid ___ too many sweets.
grammar.why: After 'avoid', use the -ing form of the verb.

grammar.q: I ___ three glasses of water so far today.
grammar.why: 'So far today' means up to now, so use the present perfect. The past participle of 'drink' is 'drunk'.

grammar.q: I ___ the flu last month, but I'm fine now.
grammar.why: 'Last month' is a finished time, so use the past simple: had.

grammar.q: ___ for half an hour a day is good for your heart.
grammar.why: When an activity is the subject of a sentence, use the -ing form: Walking is good for you.

grammar.q: Foods ___ contain a lot of sugar are bad for your teeth.
grammar.why: Use 'that' (or 'which') to say which things you mean. 'Who' is only for people.

sentences: My little brother used to hate green vegetables.
You should try to avoid sugary drinks.
Which fruit has the most vitamin C?
My doctor told me to drink more water.
Swimming is good for almost every muscle in your body.
It took me a week to recover from the flu.

reading.title: Sleep: your secret superpower
reading.text:
Most children aged 6 to 12 need between nine and twelve hours of sleep a night. That sounds like a lot, but your body and brain are very busy while you sleep.

During deep sleep, your body grows and repairs your muscles. Your brain is busy too. It sorts out what you have learnt during the day and stores the important parts, a bit like a librarian putting books on the right shelves. This is why a good night's sleep before a test can help you remember more.

If you don't get enough sleep, you may feel grumpy and find it hard to concentrate.

So how can you sleep better? Experts suggest going to bed at the same time every night. They also advise switching off phones and tablets an hour before bed, because the light from screens can make it harder to fall asleep. A calm routine, like reading a book or having a warm bath, helps your body relax.

qs.q: Why does the writer compare the brain to a librarian?
opts: It puts new information in the right order.
It reads books while you sleep.
It keeps the body quiet at night.
It only works during the day.

qs.q: Your brain stops working while you are asleep.
The light from screens can make it difficult to get to sleep.
A warm drink before bed is the best way to fall asleep.
What do experts suggest?
opts: going to bed at the same time every night
having a big meal just before bed

reading.title: Water: your body's best friend
reading.text:
About 60 per cent of your body is water. It is in your blood, your muscles and even your bones. Every day, you lose some of it when you breathe, sweat and go to the toilet, so you need to replace it.

If you don't drink enough, you may get a headache, feel tired or find it hard to concentrate. This is why many schools let pupils keep a water bottle on their desks. Experts in the UK suggest drinking six to eight glasses of liquid a day, and more when it is hot or you are doing sport.

You don't only get water from drinks. Many fruits and vegetables are full of it. A cucumber is about 95 per cent water, and a watermelon is not far behind.

Water is also the best drink for your teeth. Unlike fizzy drinks and many fruit juices, it contains no sugar. Best of all, tap water in the UK is safe to drink and very cheap.

qs.q: Why do we need to drink water every day?
opts: Our bodies lose water in several ways.
Water makes our bones grow bigger.
We cannot eat fruit without it.
It stops us from breathing too fast.

qs.q: There is water in your bones.
You can only get water from drinks.
Most pupils in the UK drink too little water at school.
According to the text, why is water good for your teeth?
opts: It has no sugar in it.

extra.q: It's important to ___ some exercise every day.
extra.why: We say 'do exercise' (or 'take exercise'). We 'play' games and sports, and we 'go' swimming or running.

extra.q: My dad is trying to ___ eating sweets after dinner.
extra.why: 'Give up' means stop doing something that you did often.

extra.q: I drink lots of water ___ it helps me to concentrate.
extra.why: 'Because' gives the reason: why do I drink lots of water? It helps me concentrate.

extra.q: I'm feeling a bit ___ today, so I'm staying at home in bed.
extra.why: 'Under the weather' means a little ill. 'Over the moon' and 'on cloud nine' mean very happy.

extra.q: Fresh fruit and vegetables are ___ to your health. (benefit)
extra.why: After 'are' we need an adjective. 'Beneficial' means good for you.

extra.q: Too much salt is bad ___ your heart.
extra.why: We say 'good for' or 'bad for' your health. 'Bad at' is about skills, as in 'bad at maths'.

sents: Eating breakfast is one of the healthiest habits you can have.
After a long night's sleep, your body needs energy to get going.
A healthy breakfast, such as porridge with fruit, gives you this energy.
It also helps you to concentrate in your morning lessons.
For these reasons, it is a bad idea to skip breakfast.
Regular exercise is good for both your body and your mind.
Firstly, it makes your heart and muscles stronger.
Secondly, it can put you in a better mood and help you to relax.
Because of these benefits, experts say that children should be active for at least an hour every day.
Walking to school or playing football with friends is an easy way to do this.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'Sugar can damage your teeth, especially if you eat sweets between meals. Fizzy drinks are also full of sugar but do not fill you up, so it is easy to have too much.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Eating too much sugar is bad for your health in more than one way.
Sweets are sold in every supermarket.
Sugar is yummy and everyone loves it!
writing.why: The paragraph gives two problems caused by sugar, so the topic sentence must introduce sugar's harmful effects. The others are off topic or chatty.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Should schools stop selling sweets and fizzy drinks? Give your opinion.' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I believe schools should stop selling sweets and fizzy drinks, because they harm pupils' teeth and health.
Fizzy drinks come in many colours and flavours.
This is an interesting question that people often talk about.
writing.why: The best thesis answers the question clearly and gives a reason. The others only give facts or say nothing about your opinion.

units.title: Festivals around the world

words.def: to do something special and enjoyable for an important day
words.ex: Families get together to ___ the new year.

words.def: something people have done in the same way for a very long time
words.ex: Eating pancakes on Shrove Tuesday is a British ___.

words.def: special clothes that make you look like a different person, animal or thing
words.ex: She wore a dragon ___ in the parade.

words.def: a line of people, bands or vehicles moving through the streets for a special day
words.ex: Thousands of people watched the ___ go through the city centre.

words.def: a small object that explodes in the sky with bright colours and loud bangs
words.ex: Each ___ lit up the night sky with red and gold.

words.def: a lamp with a cover around it, often made of paper or glass
words.ex: Each child carried a paper ___ through the dark streets.

words.def: to make something look nicer by adding pretty things to it
words.ex: Let's ___ the classroom with paper flowers.

words.def: a large group of people in one place
words.ex: A huge ___ cheered as the band marched past.

words.def: very old; from thousands of years ago
words.ex: The first Olympic Games were held in ___ Greece.

words.def: to come together in one place as a group
words.ex: On New Year's Eve, people ___ in the square to watch the clock.

words.def: a large, special meal for many people
words.ex: After the parade, the whole village shared a ___ of rice, fruit and sweets.

words.def: a special event or time
words.ex: A wedding is a happy ___ for the whole family.

words.def: a big public party in the streets, with music, dancing and people in costumes
words.ex: Our town's summer ___ has floats, steel bands and dancing in the streets.

words.def: something that people in a place usually do, often for a very long time
words.ex: In Japan, it is a ___ to take off your shoes before you go into someone's home.

words.def: the same date each year as the day when something important happened
words.ex: My grandparents had a big party for their fiftieth wedding ___.

words.def: a picture, shape or object that stands for an idea
words.ex: In many countries, a white dove is a ___ of peace.

words.def: to hold an event and welcome the people who come to it
words.ex: Our school will ___ a music festival for five other schools in June.

words.def: happening once every year
words.ex: The village holds its ___ flower show in July.

words.def: very exciting and impressive to look at
words.ex: The fireworks over the harbour at midnight were ___.

words.def: to join in an activity or event with other people
words.ex: Everyone in our class will ___ in the school concert.

grammar.q: 'I am tired,' said Mia. Mia said that she ___ tired.
grammar.why: In reported speech, the verb usually moves one step back in time: 'am' becomes 'was'.

grammar.q: My teacher ___ us that the festival starts at six.
grammar.why: 'Tell' needs a person after it (told us). 'Say' does not (she said that...).

grammar.q: During Diwali, small oil lamps ___ in windows and doorways.
grammar.why: The lamps don't light themselves; people light them. Use the passive: are + lit (plural, because 'lamps').

grammar.q: I ___ to a carnival, but I would love to go to one.
grammar.why: For experiences in your life up to now, use the present perfect: have never been.

grammar.q: The first Notting Hill Carnival ___ place in the 1960s.
grammar.why: The 1960s is a finished time, so use the past simple: took place.

grammar.q: The man ___ leads the parade plays the drums.
grammar.why: Use 'who' (or 'that') to give more information about a person.

grammar.q: The first Christmas cards ___ in London in 1843.
grammar.why: The cards didn't send anything; people sent them. Use the past passive: were + sent (plural, because 'cards').

grammar.q: In Scotland and Ireland, people ___ carve lanterns out of turnips at Halloween.
grammar.why: 'Used to' + verb describes a past habit that has changed. Today most people carve pumpkins.

grammar.q: We're looking forward to ___ the fireworks tonight.
grammar.why: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form: watching.

grammar.q: We have ___ decorated the tree, so now we can relax.
grammar.why: Use 'already' in positive sentences to say something has happened, maybe sooner than expected. 'Yet' is for questions and negatives.

sentences: Thousands of people watched the parade.
My aunt told me that the festival was amazing.
Do you know who decorated the classroom?
We have decorated the house with paper lanterns.
We are looking forward to watching the fireworks.
Thousands of dancers take part in the carnival.

reading.title: Festivals of colour and light
reading.text:
All around the world, people gather to celebrate special days. Two of the biggest festivals are Diwali and Lunar New Year.

Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated by millions of people in India and in many other countries. It usually takes place in October or November and lasts for five days. Families light small clay lamps called diyas and put them in windows and doorways. Many people also make rangoli, which are beautiful patterns on the floor made from coloured powder, rice or flower petals.

Lunar New Year usually falls in January or February. In China, it is also called the Spring Festival. Homes are decorated in red, because red is thought to be a lucky colour. Children often receive red envelopes with money inside. In the streets, crowds watch lion and dragon dances to the sound of loud drums. The celebrations end with the Lantern Festival, when thousands of lanterns light up the night.

qs.q: Diwali lasts for less than a week.
Rangoli patterns are always made from rice.
Diwali is more popular than Lunar New Year.
Why are homes decorated in red at Lunar New Year?
opts: Many people believe red brings good luck.
Red is the colour of spring.

qs.q: What is another name for Lunar New Year in China?

reading.title: A city made of ice
reading.text:
Every winter, the city of Harbin in northern China hosts one of the biggest ice festivals in the world. Winters there are long and freezing: in January, the temperature often falls below minus 20 degrees Celsius.

The festival turns this cold weather into something spectacular. Thousands of workers cut huge blocks of ice from the frozen Songhua River and carry them to the festival park. Then artists use saws and chisels to shape them. They build castles, bridges, animals and even slides that children (and adults!) can ride down.

The festival usually opens in early January and goes on until the ice begins to melt. During the day, the sculptures sparkle in the winter sunshine. At night, coloured lights inside the ice make the whole park glow red, green, blue and gold.

Visitors need to wear warm coats, thick gloves and hats, and a hot drink is always welcome.

qs.q: Where does the ice for the festival come from?
In January, it is often colder than minus 20 degrees Celsius in Harbin.
The ice festival is open all year round.
Visitors have to buy a ticket to enter the festival park.
What makes the park glow at night?

extra.q: Diwali usually takes place ___ October or November.
extra.why: Use 'in' with months, 'on' with days and dates, and 'at' with clock times.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'The festival takes place every year'?
opts: The festival happens once a year.
The festival takes a year to plan.
The festival is held every month.
extra.why: 'Takes place every year' means it happens once a year.

extra.q: The streets look beautiful with all the ___. (decorate)
extra.why: After 'all the' we need a plural noun: decorations.

extra.q: Before the parade, the children ___ their costumes to check that they fitted.
extra.why: 'Try on' means put clothes on to see if they fit.

extra.q: We ___ a great time at the carnival last weekend.
extra.why: We say 'have a good time' or 'have a great time', not 'make' or 'do' a time.

extra.q: We stayed up until midnight ___ we wanted to see the fireworks.
extra.why: 'Because' gives the reason: why did we stay up late? We wanted to see the fireworks.

sents: In Japan, the arrival of spring is celebrated with a tradition called hanami.
The name means 'looking at flowers', and it refers to the pink cherry blossom.
When this blossom appears, families and friends gather under the trees for picnics.
However, the blossom only lasts for about a week or two, so there is not much time for these picnics.
That is why people check blossom forecasts to choose the best day for their picnic.
One of the messiest festivals in the world takes place in Buñol, a small town in Spain.
It is called La Tomatina, and it is held on the last Wednesday of August.
On that day, thousands of people throw ripe tomatoes at each other for about an hour.
When the hour is over, the streets are washed clean with hoses.
It may be messy, but visitors from all over the world love it.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'Lots and lots of people came to see the parade.'?
opts: Thousands of people came to watch the parade.
Loads of people came to see the parade.
Lots of people came to see the parade, I think.
People came to the parade, like, a lot.
writing.why: 'Thousands of people' gives a clear idea of the number. 'Loads of', 'I think' and 'like, a lot' are chatty and vague.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'At Christmas, many families in Britain eat roast turkey. At Lunar New Year, Chinese families often eat dumplings, which are said to bring good luck.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: Special foods are an important part of many festivals.
A turkey is a large bird.
Food is so tasty, isn't it?
writing.why: The paragraph gives two examples of festival food, so the topic sentence must be about festival food in general. The others are off topic, too narrow or chatty.

units.title: Oceans and space

words.def: to travel around a planet, moon or star in a curved path
words.ex: The International Space Station takes about 90 minutes to ___ the Earth.

words.def: a person who is trained to travel into space
words.ex: The ___ floated around inside the space station.

words.def: the force that pulls things towards the ground or towards each other
words.ex: Because of ___, an apple falls down from a tree, not up.

words.def: the layer of gases around a planet
words.ex: The Moon has no ___, so there is no air to breathe.

words.def: the top or outside part of something
words.ex: More than two thirds of the Earth's ___ is covered by water.

words.def: to travel around a place to learn about it
words.ex: One day, people may ___ the surface of Mars.

words.def: how deep something is
words.ex: Sunlight cannot reach a ___ of more than 1,000 metres in the ocean.

words.def: the force of something pushing on something else
words.ex: Deep under the sea, the water ___ is very high, so submarines need thick walls.

words.def: any living animal, especially a strange or unusual one
words.ex: The anglerfish is a strange ___ with a light on its head.

words.def: a tool that makes things that are far away look nearer and bigger
words.ex: Through a ___, you can see craters on the Moon.

words.def: to send a rocket or spacecraft up into the sky or into space
words.ex: Engineers will ___ the rocket when the weather is calm.

words.def: an important journey or job, often into space
words.ex: The Apollo 11 ___ took the first people to the Moon in 1969.

words.def: a machine sent into space to travel around the Earth and send back information
words.ex: Weather forecasters use photos taken by a ___ high above the Earth.

words.def: a vehicle that can travel in space
words.ex: The ___ took about seven months to reach Mars.

words.def: a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together in space
words.ex: On a clear, dark night, you can see part of our ___ as a pale band of light across the sky.

words.def: a gas in the air that people and animals need in order to stay alive
words.ex: Tiny plants that float in the ocean make much of the ___ that we breathe.

words.def: the regular rise and fall of the level of the sea, which happens about twice a day
words.ex: When the ___ goes out, you can look for crabs in the rock pools.

words.def: a strong movement of water or air in one direction
words.ex: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean ___ that flows across the Atlantic.

words.def: a ship that can travel deep under the water
words.ex: Scientists used a small ___ to study the creatures on the sea floor.

words.def: extremely big
words.ex: The Pacific is a ___ ocean that covers about a third of the Earth's surface.

grammar.q: If I ___ in space, I would look at the Earth every day.
grammar.why: This is imaginary (second conditional), so use the past simple after 'if': lived.

grammar.q: If there were no gravity, everything ___ away.
grammar.why: Second conditional: if + past simple (were), then would + verb (would float).

grammar.q: The first photo of the far side of the Moon ___ in 1959.
grammar.why: The photo didn't take anything; a spacecraft took it. Use the past passive: was + taken.

grammar.q: Humans ___ on Mars yet.
grammar.why: Use the present perfect with 'yet'. 'Humans' is plural, so use 'haven't'.

grammar.q: Astronauts have to practise ___ in a huge swimming pool.
grammar.why: After 'practise', use the -ing form. ('Practise' with an 's' is the British spelling of the verb.)

grammar.q: 'I can see the whole of Africa,' said the astronaut. She said that she ___ see the whole of Africa.
grammar.why: In reported speech, 'can' usually becomes 'could'.

grammar.q: The International Space Station ___ in space since 1998.
grammar.why: With 'since', use the present perfect for something that started in the past and is still true now.

grammar.q: If the weather ___ bad tomorrow, they won't launch the rocket.
grammar.why: First conditional: after 'if', use the present simple (is), even when you talk about the future.

grammar.q: Today, much of the deep ocean ___ by robots rather than people.
grammar.why: The ocean doesn't explore anything; robots explore it. Use the present passive. 'Much of the ocean' is singular, so use 'is'.

grammar.q: Many children hope ___ astronauts when they grow up.
grammar.why: After 'hope', use 'to' + verb: hope to become.

sentences: Rockets are launched from a base in Florida.
Robots can explore the deepest parts of the ocean.
The telescope that we used belongs to my uncle.
Have astronauts ever landed on Mars?
Robots are used to explore the deep ocean.
Our Sun is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way.

reading.title: Exploring the deep
reading.text:
Space is not the only place that is hard to explore. The ocean covers more than 70 per cent of the Earth's surface, but most of it has never been explored in detail.

The deepest part of the ocean is in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific. It is about 11,000 metres deep. If you put Mount Everest at the bottom, its top would still be more than two kilometres under the water. No sunlight reaches these depths, and the water pressure is enormous: more than 1,000 times greater than at the surface. Even so, strange creatures live in the deep ocean, and many of them make their own light.

Space and the deep sea have a lot in common. Both are dark, and humans cannot survive in either place without special equipment. Astronauts wear space suits, and deep-sea explorers travel in small, very strong submarines. Today, robots do much of the exploring in both places and send photos and information back to scientists.

qs.q: How deep is the deepest part of the ocean?
Mount Everest would be completely covered by water in the Mariana Trench.
Sunlight can reach the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
Submarines cost more to build than rockets.
What does the writer say space and the deep sea have in common?
opts: Humans need special equipment to survive in both.

reading.title: A day on the space station
reading.text:
About 400 kilometres above our heads, the International Space Station travels around the Earth at about 28,000 kilometres an hour. Because it completes an orbit every 90 minutes, the astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises every day!

Life in space is strange. Because everything floats, nothing stays where you put it, so tools, pens and food packets are fixed to the walls with Velcro. At night, astronauts sleep in sleeping bags that are tied to the wall, so they don't drift around and bump into things.

Staying healthy takes hard work. In space, muscles and bones get weaker because they do not have to hold up the body. To stop this, astronauts exercise for about two hours every day on special machines.

Water is precious, too. Almost all the water on the station is recycled, including the water in the astronauts' breath and sweat. It is cleaned so carefully that they can drink it again.

qs.q: Why do astronauts on the station see about 16 sunrises a day?
opts: The station goes around the Earth every 90 minutes.
The Sun is much closer to the station.
The astronauts sleep for only 90 minutes.
The station has very big windows.

qs.q: Astronauts on the station sleep in normal beds.
Astronauts exercise for about two hours a day.
Most astronauts stay on the station for about six months.
Why are tools and pens fixed to the walls?
opts: so that they do not float away
so that astronauts can find them in the dark
so that they do not get too cold

extra.q: Three, two, one... and the rocket ___!
extra.why: 'Take off' means leave the ground and rise into the air.

extra.q: Which sentence comes next? 'The Moon has no air. ___'
opts: Because of this, astronauts must wear space suits there.
However, there is lots of air on the Moon.
For example, the Earth is round.
extra.why: 'Because of this' links a cause (there is no air) to its result (astronauts need space suits).

extra.q: ___ the Moon looks small, it is about a quarter as wide as the Earth.
extra.why: 'Although' joins two ideas that are surprising together: it looks small, but it is quite big.

extra.q: Space ___ costs a lot of money. (explore)
extra.why: We need a noun for the activity: exploration. An 'explorer' is a person.

extra.q: From the space station, the astronaut ___ a photo of her home town.
extra.why: We say 'take a photo' (or 'take a picture'), not 'make' or 'do' a photo.

extra.q: The space station travels ___ the Earth every 90 minutes.
extra.why: Something in orbit moves around (or round) a planet, in a circle.

sents: The first Moon landing in 1969 was one of the greatest moments in the history of exploration.
On 20 July, Apollo 11's lunar module, called Eagle, landed on the Moon's surface.
A few hours later, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon.
He was soon followed by Buzz Aldrin, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
Millions of people around the world watched these events live on television.
The tides in the sea are caused mainly by the Moon.
As the Moon travels around the Earth, its gravity pulls on the oceans.
This pull makes the sea rise in some places and fall in others.
As a result, the sea on most coasts rises and falls about twice a day.
So the next time you are at the seaside, remember that the Moon is moving the water.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Some people think that more money should be spent on exploring space. Others think it should be spent on problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your opinion.' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: Although exploring space teaches us a great deal, I believe money should first be spent on problems on Earth, such as protecting the oceans.
Space is very big and full of stars.
Rockets are expensive and they look cool.
There are two views about this question.
writing.why: The best thesis mentions both views and gives a clear opinion. The others do not answer the question.

writing.q: Read the rest of a paragraph: 'The ocean covers more than 70 per cent of the Earth's surface, but most of it has never been explored in detail. Many deep-sea creatures have not even been given names yet.' Which topic sentence fits best?
opts: We still know surprisingly little about the ocean.
The ocean is wet and salty.
Space is easier to explore than the sea.
writing.why: Both sentences show how much of the ocean is still unknown. The others are too obvious, about space or about the writer.

units.title: Money and shopping

words.def: a plan for how much money you can spend and what you will spend it on
words.ex: We set a ___ of £20 for the birthday party.

words.def: something you buy for much less than its usual price
words.ex: At only £3, this warm winter coat was a real ___.

words.def: an amount of money taken off the usual price
words.ex: Students get a 10 per cent ___ at the museum shop.

words.def: money that a shop gives back to you when you return something
words.ex: The toy was broken, so the shop gave us a full ___.

words.def: a piece of paper that shows what you bought and how much you paid
words.ex: Keep the ___ in case you need to take the shirt back.

words.def: to buy something (a more formal word)
words.ex: You can ___ tickets online or at the door.

words.def: to give something to someone for a short time and expect to get it back
words.ex: Could you ___ me your pen for a minute?

words.def: the kind of money that is used in a country
words.ex: The euro is the ___ of many countries in Europe.

words.def: to take something back to a shop and get a different thing instead
words.ex: Can I ___ these jeans for a bigger size?

words.def: to look at two or more things to see how they are similar or different
words.ex: Always ___ prices before you buy something expensive.

words.def: the name of a product made by a particular company
words.ex: This ___ of trainers is very popular with teenagers.

words.def: owned by someone else before you
words.ex: I bought a ___ bike, and it works perfectly.

words.def: a line of people who are waiting for something
words.ex: We waited in a ___ for twenty minutes to buy ice cream.

words.def: to take things such as letters or shopping to someone's home
words.ex: The shop will ___ our new sofa on Friday.

words.def: having a particular value in money
words.ex: This old comic is now ___ more than £100.

words.def: an organisation that collects money to help people or animals in need
words.ex: Our class raised £200 for a ___ that protects wild birds.

words.def: to give money or things to help others, often through an organisation
words.ex: Every month, I ___ a little of my pocket money to an animal charity.

words.def: the money that you get every month for doing your job
words.ex: My aunt's ___ is paid into her bank account at the end of each month.

words.def: how much something is worth
words.ex: The ___ of an old coin depends on how rare it is.

words.def: completely necessary; something you must have
words.ex: Bread and milk are ___ items that most families buy every week.

grammar.q: I ___ enough money for a new bike yet.
grammar.why: Use the present perfect with 'yet' for something that hasn't happened up to now. 'I' goes with 'haven't'.

grammar.q: Last Saturday, we ___ a second-hand bike at the market.
grammar.why: 'Last Saturday' is a finished time, so use the past simple: bought.

grammar.q: If I ___ a lot of money, I would buy a house by the sea for my parents.
grammar.why: This is imaginary (second conditional), so use the past simple after 'if' (won), then would + verb.

grammar.q: If you ___ your receipt, the shop will give you a refund.
grammar.why: First conditional: if + present simple (keep), then will + verb. Don't use 'will' after 'if'.

grammar.q: In the UK, coins ___ by the Royal Mint in Wales.
grammar.why: The coins don't make anything; the Royal Mint makes them. Use the present passive: are + made (plural, because 'coins').

grammar.q: The first paper money ___ in China about 1,000 years ago.
grammar.why: Use the past passive for a finished time. 'Money' is uncountable, so use 'was', not 'were'.

grammar.q: People ___ pay for everything with coins and notes, but now many use cards or phones.
grammar.why: 'Used to' + verb describes a past habit that is not true now.

grammar.q: 'I want to save my money,' said Ben. Ben said that he ___ to save his money.
grammar.why: In reported speech, the present simple (want) usually moves back to the past simple (wanted).

grammar.q: My sister is saving up ___ a new phone.
grammar.why: Use 'to' + verb to give the purpose: she is saving up so that she can buy a phone.

grammar.q: A charity shop is a shop ___ sells things that people have given away.
grammar.why: Use 'that' (or 'which') to say which shop you mean. 'Where' would need a subject after it: a shop where people sell things.

sentences: This jumper was a bargain in the sales.
British coins are made by the Royal Mint.
My sister is saving up to buy a new phone.
A charity shop sells things that people have donated.
Have you ever bought anything second-hand?
The supermarket queue was very long.

reading.title: The story of money
reading.text:
Long ago, before money was invented, people who wanted something had to swap. A farmer might exchange a bag of grain for a pair of shoes. But this was not always easy. What if the shoemaker did not want any grain?

To solve this problem, people began to use objects that everyone agreed were valuable. In parts of Africa and Asia, small, shiny cowrie shells were used as money for centuries.

The first coins were made about 2,600 years ago in Lydia, in what is now Turkey. Coins were small, strong and easy to carry. Later, about 1,000 years ago, paper money was used for the first time in China. It was much lighter than a heavy bag of coins.

Today, money is changing again. In many countries, people pay with cards or phones, and some shops no longer accept cash at all. Who knows what money will look like in the future?

qs.q: Why was swapping not always easy?
opts: The other person might not want what you had.
Farmers did not grow any grain.

qs.q: Shells were once used as money in some parts of the world.
The first coins were made in China.
Gold coins were worth more than paper money.
What was one advantage of paper money?
opts: It could only be used in Turkey.

reading.title: The secrets of the supermarket
reading.text:
Have you ever gone to the supermarket for a pint of milk and come home with a full bag? If so, you are not alone. Supermarkets are carefully designed to make us buy more.

For example, everyday items such as milk and bread are often placed at the back of the shop. To reach them, customers have to walk past hundreds of other products, and many people pick up something they had not planned to buy.

Prices are also chosen carefully. A price of £1.99 seems much lower than £2, even though the difference is only one penny. Sweets used to be displayed near the tills, where children waiting in the queue could easily see them. In England, large shops are no longer allowed to do this.

Knowing these tricks can help you to save money. Before you go shopping, write a list and decide how much you want to spend. Then stick to your budget!

qs.q: What is the main idea of the text?
opts: Supermarkets use clever tricks to make us spend more.

qs.q: Milk and bread are often found near the entrance of the shop.
A price ending in 99 can make something seem cheaper.
Most people spend more at the supermarket on Saturdays.
What does the writer advise you to do before you go shopping?
opts: Write a list and set a budget.
Go when you are very hungry.
Take a younger brother or sister.
Only buy things from the back of the shop.

extra.q: Can I ___ by card, please?
extra.why: We say 'pay by card' or 'pay in cash'. You 'buy' a thing and 'spend' money.

extra.q: How much did you spend ___ your new trainers?
extra.why: We 'spend money on' something.

extra.q: I'm ___ a birthday present for my dad. Have you got any ideas?
extra.why: 'Look for' means try to find something.

extra.q: Thank you for your kind ___ to the school fair. (donate)
extra.why: After 'your kind' we need a noun for the thing you gave: donation. A 'donor' is a person.

extra.q: I wanted to buy the game, ___ I didn't have enough money.
extra.why: 'But' joins two ideas that go against each other: I wanted it, but I couldn't pay.

extra.q: Which sentence means the same as 'These shoes were a bargain'?
opts: These shoes cost less than they usually do.
extra.why: A 'bargain' is something that you buy for less than its usual price.

sents: Many parents give their children pocket money every week.
This helps children to learn how to manage money.
For example, they may need to save for several weeks to buy something special.
In this way, they learn that they cannot have everything at once.
These are lessons that will be useful for the rest of their lives.
Charity shops are a great place to find a bargain.
They sell clothes, books and toys that people have given away.
Because the shop gets these things for free, it can sell them at low prices.
The money it makes is then used to help people or animals in need.
So when you shop there, you save money and help others at the same time.

writing.q: Which is the most precise way to say: 'The price of the game went down a bit in the sale.'?
opts: The price of the game fell slightly in the sale.
The game got a bit cheaper, kind of.
The price of the game went down loads.
The game's price did a small drop.
writing.why: 'Fell slightly' is short and exact. 'Kind of' is vague, 'loads' is chatty and changes the meaning, and 'did a small drop' is not natural English.

writing.q: Essay question: 'Should children get pocket money for helping at home? Give your opinion.' Which is the clearest thesis statement?
opts: I think children should get pocket money for helping at home, because it teaches them that work has value.
Pocket money is money that children get.
My friend gets five pounds a week.
Helping at home can mean many different things.
writing.why: The best thesis answers the question and gives a reason. The others only explain a word, tell a story or stay vague.
